class.name: CameraAttributes
class.description: Controls camera-specific attributes such as depth of field and exposure override. When used in a [WorldEnvironment] it provides default settings for exposure, auto-exposure, and depth of field that will be used by all cameras without their own [CameraAttributes], including the editor camera. When used in a [Camera3D] it will override any [CameraAttributes] set in the [WorldEnvironment]. When used in [VoxelGI] or [LightmapGI], only the exposure settings will be used. See also [Environment] for general 3D environment settings. This is a pure virtual class that is inherited by [CameraAttributesPhysical] and [CameraAttributesPractical].

members.member: How much more the middle of the screen counts than its edges when auto exposure measures the scene's brightness. [code]0[/code] measures the whole screen equally. A higher value makes exposure follow what the camera is pointed at, so a flashlight beam in a dark corridor keeps the corridor dark instead of being averaged away, and exposure stops pumping when the view sweeps over bright or dark edges. The measurement stays an average, so the overall brightness does not change when the scene is evenly lit.

A multiplier on [member auto_exposure_speed] that applies only while the scene gets darker, that is while exposure is rising. Eyes adjust to bright light within a moment but take much longer to adjust to darkness, so a value below [code]1[/code], such as [code]0.2[/code], makes the image stay dark for a few seconds after the lights go out and then slowly fade up, and still snap back quickly when the lights come on. [code]1[/code] adapts at the same speed in both directions.

If [code]true[/code], enables the tonemapping auto exposure mode of the scene renderer. If [code]true[/code], the renderer will automatically determine the exposure setting to adapt to the scene's illumination and the observed light. [b]Note:[/b] Auto-exposure is only supported in the Forward+ rendering method, not Mobile or Compatibility.
The scale of the auto exposure effect. Affects the intensity of auto exposure.
The speed of the auto exposure effect. Affects the time needed for the camera to perform auto exposure. See also [member auto_exposure_dark_speed], which slows this down while the scene gets darker.
Multiplier for the exposure amount. A higher value results in a brighter image.

Sensitivity of camera sensors, measured in ISO. A higher sensitivity results in a brighter image. If [member auto_exposure_enabled] is [code]true[/code], this can be used as a method of exposure compensation, doubling the value will increase the exposure value (measured in EV100) by 1 stop. [b]Note:[/b] Only available when [member ProjectSettings.rendering/lights_and_shadows/use_physical_light_units] is enabled.
How quickly the focus moves to the distance of what is looked at, with [member gaze_focus_depth_range]. Higher refocuses faster; [code]0.0[/code] refocuses at once.
How blurred what is out of focus gets, from [code]0.0[/code] to [code]1.0[/code].

If above [code]0.0[/code], what is nearer or further than the looked-at thing by this many metres is blurred too, even right next to the gaze, the way eyes focus on one distance. [code]0.0[/code] blurs only by distance from the gaze on the screen.

If [code]true[/code], keeps what the player looks at sharp and blurs the rest of the view, following [EyeTracker] (or the middle of the screen without it). The gaze point of a viewport can also be set with [method RenderingServer.viewport_set_gaze_point]. [b]Note:[/b] Only supported in the Forward+ renderer.
How far from the gaze stays fully sharp, as a part of the screen's height.
Over how much more, as a part of the screen's height, the blur fades in past [member gaze_focus_radius].

If [code]true[/code], things that move across the screen are smeared along the way they move, as they are by a camera's shutter. The camera's own motion counts, a turn or a run blurs the whole view including the sky, and so does the motion of every object, so a car blurs against a still background and a still car blurs against a moving camera. It is made from the velocity buffer, the one temporal anti-aliasing uses, so it follows whatever the renderer drew: skeletons, instanced meshes and moving lights included. It works on the HDR image before glow and tonemapping, so a bright thing leaves a bright streak, and what is in front smears over what is behind it, not the other way about. [b]Note:[/b] Motion blur is only available in the Forward+ renderer. It needs a camera and a frame before it: nothing blurs on the first frame of a game or after the camera was moved by hand to somewhere new, until the next frame says how it moved.

How much of the time between frames the shutter is open, from [code]0[/code] to [code]1[/code]. At [code]0.5[/code], a half shutter, a thing is smeared over half of what it moved in the frame, which is what film cameras do (a 180 degree shutter). At [code]1[/code] it is smeared over all of it.

The longest a streak may be, as a percentage of the screen's width. Faster things are smeared no further, so a hard turn doesn't turn the screen to soup. Up to about 6.7% on a 1080p screen is possible; more is cut to what the blur can reach.
How many samples are taken along a streak. More are smoother and cost more.

The frame rate the blur is made for. A velocity is how far a pixel moved in a frame, which is less the faster the game runs, so with this set the streak is scaled to the length it would be at this rate: the game looks the same at 60 frames a second and at 144. At [code]0[/code] the blur is scaled by [member motion_blur_intensity] alone, and gets shorter as the frame rate rises.
